clue.text: Unsuccessful with money? This’ll get you a raise!

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the answer, a bread that rises

blocks.note: a plan that goes sour has failed
dough is slang for cash

explanation.surface: Someone short of cash is told this is the way to win a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'raise' wanted is not a pay rise but the rising of a loaf; dough doubles as money and as bread mix, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Sourdough is a fermented starter that leavens bread, making the loaf rise in the oven.

clue.text: Band who had Christmas hit broadcast rode with Santa?

indicators.note: what is broadcast is heard on air rather than seen in print

blocks.note: Slade, the British glam-rock band, had the perennial hit Merry Xmas Everybody

explanation.walkthrough: Slade is a 1970s British rock band whose Merry Xmas Everybody is replayed every December; its name is said just like the answer.

clue.text: Head covering, apparently worn on top in city

explanation.surface: A hat that seems to be worn high on the head by people in town.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke reads the headdress as a T sitting on top of the answer, so take that T away.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes things belonging to or located within a town or city environment.

clue.text: Sensible, with gravity?

blocks.note: first meaning: practical and realistic
second meaning, read literally: gravity pulls everything towards the planet's surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'With gravity' looks like 'seriously', but it means the physical force that brings falling things to the ground.

clue.text: Jack abandoning boat and gathering up fish to leave port

a common sea fish

explanation.walkthrough: Drop J from JUNK to get UNK, then insert the fish turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Undocking is releasing a vessel from its berth so that it can move away from the harbour.

clue.text: Flailing about, loses speech — a non-starter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' that looks like part of the definition is in fact the last letter of the fodder.

clue.text: One’s back with writer touring about in hired vehicle

clue.text: Sun follower looked rich

blocks.note: Monday follows Sunday; MON is its abbreviation
to eye something is to look at it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun follower' suggests a sunflower or sunbather; it is the day after Sunday.

clue.text: Officer and soldiers confined to station — one’s gone upstairs

clue.text: Trust one in suit to have means of paying

clue.text: Start in college of western America where pupils are trained?

clue.text: Banishes darkness from swamp lands

a bird that lights on a branch lands there

clue.text: Hang around sides of playing surface for curling

clue.text: Registers omen hanging over child

indicators.note: in a down entry, hanging above means coming first

blocks.note: an omen is a sign of things to come
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A bad omen looms over a child in some superstitious tale.

clue.text: Possessing joint, tested nudge theory, perhaps

clue.text: Punishment not unknown in west country town

algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

clue.text: Regarding who sits on throne?

explanation.surface: A question about who occupies the throne.

clue.text: It’s made in lab, I tell agency cryptically

indicators.note: a cryptic arrangement is a puzzling, scrambled one, so the letters are reworked

the setter's comment that these letters have been altered, written into the entry

explanation.walkthrough: The second word of the answer describes the first: the eleven letters of 'I tell agency', modified, spell the first word.

clue.text: Island floors

blocks.note: first meaning: a Greek island in the Dodecanese
second meaning: knocks out, as a boxer does an opponent

explanation.walkthrough: 'Floors' looks like a noun but is a verb: to floor someone is to knock them down.

clue.text: Refuse tablets to take orally

blocks.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so tablets are Es
to chew is to work food in the mouth

explanation.surface: A patient declines the pills meant to be swallowed.

clue.text: Alleged medical blunders

indicators.note: a blunder is a mistake, so the letters come out wrongly ordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Medical blunders' reads as a noun phrase, but 'blunders' is the verb acting on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something alleged has been asserted without proof, which is what a claimed fact is.

clue.text: Exhausted, due to change in unique selling point

indicators.note: changing something alters it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: USP is the marketing abbreviation for unique selling point
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: USP is a marketing term; the rearranged short word goes between its second and third letters.

clue.text: Prisoner, not “caught” in a manner of speaking, in nick

clue.text: Eddy, rejecting kiss in embrace of rascal, was frolicking

clue.text: I’m not sure this is a secret

clue.text: Unaccompanied royal’s autobiography?

explanation.definitionFit: The prickly plant is Scotland's national emblem and produces fluffy seed tufts called thistledown.

clue.text: One to bat — watch stroke

blocks.note: to eye is to watch
a lash is a stroke of the whip

explanation.surface: A cricketer waiting to go in watches a fine shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bat' and 'stroke' summon cricket, but to bat an eyelid is to flutter it.
explanation.definitionFit: People bat their eyelashes when flirting, so a lash is the thing that gets batted.

clue.text: During work duties, I carouse

indicators.note: something during an event happens within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a roster lists who is on duty when
taken as written

explanation.surface: An employee confesses to partying while on shift.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a confession; the I is simply the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To roister is to revel noisily and boisterously, the same as to carouse.

clue.text: Stopped working around mid-evening and had a meal

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter
to go around is to enclose

blocks.note: a machine that died stopped working
the central letter of seven

explanation.surface: Someone knocked off work in the evening and ate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopped working' sounds like finishing a shift, but it is what a broken machine does.
explanation.definitionFit: To dine is to eat a meal, usually the main evening one, so dined means ate.

clue.text: Miss Havisham‘s dresses tell all when discovered

definitions.note: a possessive standing for her ward

indicators.note: to dis-cover is to strip the coverings, exposing what lies within the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: The jilted bride's old wedding dresses reveal her whole story once found.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Havisham, the jilted recluse of Dickens's Great Expectations, raised a girl to break men's hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: Estella is Miss Havisham's adopted daughter in Great Expectations, so she is Miss Havisham's girl.

clue.text: Mark house and pass on

blocks.note: a semi is a semi-detached house, joined to its neighbour
a col is a mountain pass
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notes the house before moving on, or dying.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is British shorthand for a semi-detached house; 'pass on' looks like a single verb but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: A semicolon is a punctuation mark, one of the marks used in writing to divide clauses.
